strengths: First application of inversion-free editing paradigm to video editing with T2V models, addressing real limitations of inversion-based methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics and strong performance: outperforms baselines on CLIP-T (33.72 vs 32.93), CLIP-F (98.37 vs 97.13), Frame-Acc (84.38 vs 77.82), and achieves best Qedit
Well-motivated technical approach with elegant noise-cancellation mechanism through shared noise instances between source and target velocities
Non-intrusive SAFC design that operates externally to model architecture, enhancing generality and adaptability across different T2V models
Extensive qualitative validation with diverse editing scenarios (Figures 9-16) demonstrating practical effectiveness across object editing, texture transformation, and attribute modification
Significant computational efficiency gains: DAG achieves comparable results in 5 minutes versus 29 minutes for conventional averaging on 41-frame videos
Training-free approach with promised code release providing immediate practical value
Honest discussion of limitations including text replacement sensitivity and style transfer constraints
Reasonable ablation studies demonstrating contribution of SAFC and DAG components
weaknesses: Critical structural preservation trade-off: achieves lowest WarpSSIM score (57.69) versus best baseline (72.64), indicating substantial loss of structural fidelity despite claims of structure preservation

Severe practical limitation from text prompt dependency: method fails significantly when source prompt descriptions persist in target prompt (Appendix F), limiting usability without explicit prompt engineering guidance
Generalization concerns: all experiments exclusively on Wan 2.1 model; cross-attention extraction requires model-specific tuning; unclear how SAFC adapts to different attention architectures
Limited technical novelty: core ODE editing adapted from concurrent FlowEdit [24], SAFC applies established attention-guided masking, DAG uses standard CFG principles differentially

Insufficient ablation and hyperparameter analysis: introduces multiple parameters (L_HQ, L_BL, w, smoothing kernel n, decay factor δ) without sensitivity studies, justification, or comprehensive ablations

Theoretical justification gaps: velocity field averaging principle lacks rigorous analysis, validity of constructed Z_tar as true target intermediate state not formally established, mask generation heuristics (smoothing + thresholding) lack principled foundation

Narrow evaluation scope: single T2V model tested, relatively simple video scenarios, maximum 36 frames, no user studies, computational cost comparisons with baselines absent, long-video scalability unclear

Reproducibility limitations: architecture-dependent cross-attention extraction, implementation details scattered across appendices, no guidance for adapting to new models, potential brittleness of heuristic thresholds
Incomplete ablations: single SAFC example (Figure 5), no analysis of averaging sample count sensitivity, no investigation of failure modes beyond text replacement
